question: What will the Antarctic sea ice extent be on October 11, 2026, according to the NSIDC Sea Ice Index?
resolution_criteria: Resolves to the daily Antarctic sea ice extent for 2026-10-11 in the NSIDC Sea Ice Index version 4 daily file (S_seaice_extent_daily_v4.0.csv), in millions of square kilometers.
research:
I couldn't confirm any forecast or news published by 2026-09-20 that is relevant here. The NSIDC daily file puts extent at **17.366 M km² on 2026-09-20**, about 0.25 below the season-to-date peak of 17.619 on 2026-09-11. Over 2018 to 2025, extent fell between Sep 20 and Oct 11 in every year, by an average of about 0.31.

## 1. Resolution source
- The source is the NSIDC Sea Ice Index v4 daily file, [S_seaice_extent_daily_v4.0.csv](https://noaadata.apps.nsidc.org/NOAA/G02135/south/daily/data/S_seaice_extent_daily_v4.0.csv). I read it in chunks and copied the values below from it. Recent days are near-real-time and may be revised slightly. On 2026-09-20 itself, that day's value may not yet have been published, since the file usually runs about a day behind.
- 2026-09-20: 17.366. Prior days: Sep 19: 17.342, Sep 18: 17.303, Sep 17: 17.344, Sep 16: 17.382, Sep 15: 17.480, Sep 14: 17.613, Sep 11: 17.619 (highest so far), Sep 1: 17.415, Aug 20: 16.490. [NSIDC CSV](https://noaadata.apps.nsidc.org/NOAA/G02135/south/daily/data/S_seaice_extent_daily_v4.0.csv)
- The file's source column shows that in 2025 the near-real-time input switched from NSIDC-0051 to NSIDC-0803 (AMSR2). Values before and after that switch may not be perfectly comparable.

## 2. Current status
- Nothing settles the question yet; the answer depends on 21 more days of change. The seasonal maximum looks likely to have passed around Sep 11-14, at roughly 17.6. Ice has been flat to slightly rising since Sep 18.
- 2026-09-20: the value of 17.366 sits inside the question's range of 16.5 to 18.5.

## 3. Recent news (newest first)
- 2026-09-20: I found no NSIDC "Sea Ice Today" post or other news about the Antarctic maximum dated on or before Sep 20.
- A Met Office briefing and NASA and other coverage exist, but they were published after the cutoff, so I have left them out.

## 4. Base rates and seasonal comparison
From the same file:

| Year | Sep 20 | Oct 11 | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2018 | 18.175 | 18.045 | -0.130 |
| 2019 | 18.232 | 18.225 | -0.007 |
| 2020 | 18.870 | 18.628 | -0.242 |
| 2021 | 18.429 | 17.830 | -0.599 |
| 2022 | 18.177 | 17.927 | -0.250 |
| 2023 | 16.841 | 16.377 | -0.464 |
| 2024 | 17.197 | 16.809 | -0.388 |
| 2025 | 17.671 | 17.274 | -0.397 |

- In all 8 years, extent fell between Sep 20 and Oct 11. The average fall was about -0.31, ranging from -0.01 to -0.60. The last three years (2023-2025) fell by more: -0.39 to -0.46.
- If you apply that historical range of changes to 17.366, you get roughly 16.77 to 17.36. The average change gives about 17.06; the 2023-2025 changes give about 16.90 to 16.98. This is simple arithmetic, not a forecast.
- 2026 is running above 2023 (16.841) and 2024 (17.197) for Sep 20, but below 2025 (17.671) and every year from 2018 to 2022. In practice that makes it third-lowest for this date in the recent record.
- Peaks for comparison: 2023 peaked at 17.109 on Sep 7 in this file (NSIDC's official record-low maximum is 16.96 M km², on 10 Sep 2023). 2024 peaked at 17.283 on Sep 15 and 2025 at 17.854 on Sep 15. 2026's highest so far is 17.619 on Sep 11.
- How the path to Oct 11 varied:
  - 2023 rose slightly to 16.867 on Sep 30, then fell fast in October.
  - 2024 went back up to 17.275 on Sep 30, then dropped about 0.47 in 11 days.
  - Late-September rebounds of 0.1-0.3 have happened (2019, 2020, 2024).
  - In early October, extent typically falls about 0.03-0.05 per day.

## 5. Other forecasts
- I found no Polymarket, Kalshi or Manifold market on this question, and no expert forecast of Antarctic extent for Oct 11, 2026.

## 6. Upcoming events before resolution
- NSIDC usually announces the Antarctic maximum in late September or early October. A late-September rebound could, in principle, push the season's peak above the Sep 11 value.
- Weather: the main drivers are Southern Ocean winds and storms, especially the Southern Annular Mode, which pushes ice outward or packs it together. I found no official sea-ice outlook covering the period up to Oct 11, 2026.
- Near-real-time values can be revised slightly, and the Oct 11 value should appear in the file around Oct 12.

Sources:
- [NSIDC S_seaice_extent_daily_v4.0.csv](https://noaadata.apps.nsidc.org/NOAA/G02135/south/daily/data/S_seaice_extent_daily_v4.0.csv)
